body:
Rationale for this change
add_files looks up each Parquet column path in a mapping built from the table's current column names, so a file that is valid for the table fails when its paths differ from those names:
catalog.create_table("db.t", schema=Schema(NestedField(1, "a", LongType()), NestedField(2, "b", StringType())))
with catalog.load_table("db.t").update_schema() as update:
    update.rename_column("a", "c")
# The file has field IDs 1 and 2, and column 1 is still named "a" in it.
catalog.load_table("db.t").add_files(["a.parquet"])  # KeyError: 'a'
The same happens for a nested field renamed after the file was written (KeyError: 'address.zip') and for a list whose element is named item, the layout pyarrow writes with use_compliant_nested_type=False (KeyError: 'tags.list.item'). #716 reported the list case; the stale bot closed it without a fix.
The name-based mapping can also record statistics under the wrong column. If the table drops a (field ID 1) and adds a new a (field ID 3), an old file's a is recorded under field ID 3, so a scan for a IS NULL prunes the file and misses its rows.
This change builds the mapping from the file's own column paths and field IDs (with name mapping for files without IDs), so statistics follow field IDs as they do for files PyIceberg writes.
Are these changes tested?
Yes, in tests/io/test_pyarrow.py. test_add_files_matches_columns_by_field_id covers the nested rename and the item list element with and without field IDs. test_add_files_with_field_ids_swapped_relative_to_names covers a file whose a and b have each other's field IDs, where filters on either column pruned the file. test_add_files_rejects_columns_missing_from_table covers a file column whose field ID the table lacks, including a dropped column whose name a new column reuses. All three fail without this change.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes:

add_files accepts files whose columns were renamed in the table and files whose list element is not named element.
A file column whose field ID is not in the table now gets the existing "PyArrow table contains more columns" ValueError instead of a KeyError.
A file column whose field ID was dropped from the table is rejected with the same error, even when a new column reuses its name. Before, such a file was added with its statistics under the new column.
A file whose column names are swapped relative to their field IDs gets its statistics by field ID, so filters no longer prune it.

This pull request and its description were written by Isaac.
title: Map add_files columns by the file's own field IDs

body:
Rationale for this change
Table.append fails for a table identity-partitioned on a uuid column:
schema = Schema(NestedField(1, "id", LongType()), NestedField(2, "u", UUIDType()))
tbl = catalog.create_table("db.t", schema=schema, partition_spec=PartitionSpec(PartitionField(2, 1000, IdentityTransform(), "u")))
tbl.append(pa.table({"id": pa.array([1], pa.int64()), "u": pa.array([uuid.UUID(int=1).bytes], pa.uuid())}))
# pyarrow.lib.ArrowNotImplementedError: Keys of type extension<arrow.uuid>
The identity transform returns the arrow.uuid column unchanged, and PyArrow has no group by or equality kernel for extension types, so the group_by in _determine_partitions fails before any file is written. Bucketing on the uuid column works because the bucket transform returns an int.
This change groups and filters on the storage type of extension-typed partition columns (fixed_size_binary(16) for uuid). PyArrow does not plan compute kernels for extension types (apache/arrow#39024 was closed as not planned), so this stays needed. The data columns are unchanged, so the Parquet files keep the uuid type, and the partition values are the 16 bytes the manifests store for a uuid.
Not changed here: an equality filter on a uuid identity partition still plans no files, because partition pruning compares the UUID read from the manifest with a bytes literal. That also affects tables written by other engines, and I'll send it as a separate fix.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. Two new tests in tests/io/test_pyarrow.py fail with ArrowNotImplementedError: Keys of type extension<arrow.uuid> without this change and pass with it, on pyarrow 25 and 18:

test_determine_partitions_with_uuid_column: the partition keys (including a null partition), the rows of each partition, and that the data keeps the uuid type.
test_append_uuid_to_table_partitioned_on_uuid: an append through the catalog fixture, the rows read back, and the partition values of the data files.

Are there any user-facing changes?
Bug fix only: appending to a table identity-partitioned on a uuid column no longer raises. No API change.
This pull request and its description were written by Isaac.

body:
Rationale for this change
Table.snapshot_as_of_timestamp walks the snapshot log backwards and returns the first entry at or before the timestamp, which assumes the log is ordered by timestamp. The spec does not guarantee that, and Java's TableMetadata accepts a log entry up to one minute older than the previous one, so inside that skew window the lookup can return an older snapshot. Java fixed the same assumption in SnapshotUtil.nullableSnapshotIdAsOfTime (apache/iceberg#17360, "finding the entry with the maximum timestamp <= requested timestamp").
This picks the entry with the largest timestamp that is at or before (or strictly before, with inclusive=False) the requested one. On equal timestamps the later entry wins, unlike Java which keeps the first: PyIceberg logs every snapshot added in one transaction with its own timestamp_ms, so two can share a millisecond and the later one is the state that was actually current. Later-wins is also what PyIceberg and Java did before. inspect.metadata_log_entries uses the same lookup for latest_snapshot_id.
Are these changes tested?
Yes, test_snapshot_by_timestamp_with_unordered_snapshot_log in tests/table/test_init.py (two entries 10 seconds out of order, plus a tie; fails on main, passes here). tests/table/test_init.py and tests/table/test_inspect.py pass.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Time travel by timestamp returns the right snapshot when the snapshot log has entries slightly out of timestamp order.
title: Pick the latest timestamp in snapshot_as_of_timestamp instead of the last log entry

Rationale for this change
When a snapshot is removed (RemoveSnapshotsUpdate, which expire_snapshots uses), pyiceberg removes the snapshot's statistics files but keeps its partition statistics files. After expiring a snapshot, the table metadata still has partition-statistics entries pointing at a snapshot that is gone.
Iceberg Java removes both in TableMetadata.Builder.rewriteSnapshotsInternal:
removeStatistics(snapshotId);
removePartitionStatistics(snapshotId);
This adds the same removal for partition statistics, next to the existing one for statistics. A REST catalog server applies the update itself, so you mostly see this with catalogs where pyiceberg writes the metadata (SQL, Glue, Hive, DynamoDB). body:
Rationale for this change
Scan planning gets uuid identity partitions wrong. On a table partitioned by identity(u) on a uuid column:
tbl.scan(row_filter=EqualTo("u", str(first))).plan_files()  # no files; count() is 0
tbl.scan(row_filter=In("u", {str(first), str(second)})).plan_files()  # no files
tbl.scan(row_filter=NotEqualTo("u", str(first))).count()  # counts the excluded partition too
PyIceberg has two in-memory representations of a uuid: the Avro UUIDReader returns a uuid.UUID, so the partition values read from manifests are UUID, while UUIDLiteral and from_bytes(UUIDType) use the 16 bytes. The partition and residual evaluators compare a UUID with bytes and never find them equal, and so does the filter on an identity partition value projected into a data file that does not contain the column.
This change standardizes on uuid.UUID, as Java does (UUIDLiteral is a Literal<UUID>, and Conversions.fromByteBuffer returns a UUID):

UUIDLiteral wraps a uuid.UUID. literal(), StringLiteral.to(UUIDType), FixedLiteral.to(UUIDType) and BinaryLiteral.to(UUIDType) build one, and UUIDLiteral.to(FixedType) and to(BinaryType) convert back with .bytes.
from_bytes(UUIDType) returns a uuid.UUID, so the metrics evaluators compare the lower and upper bounds as UUID.
_to_partition_representation(UUIDType) keeps identity partition values as UUID.
PyArrow gets the 16 bytes for uuid filter scalars and IN and NOT IN lists; PyArrow 18 rejects a uuid.UUID there.

Ordering is unchanged: UUID compares by its integer value, which matches the unsigned big-endian byte order, so range predicates and min/max pruning keep working. The conversion in the scan planner from the first version of this PR is gone.
Follow-up to #4360. When a uuid predicate reaches PyArrow against a uuid column stored in a data file, to_arrow() still raises the ArrowNotImplementedError of #2372, and so does count() when it has to read the rows. For = and in filters on matching identity partitions, this replaces silently returning no rows.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. In tests/io/test_pyarrow.py, test_scan_plans_uuid_identity_partitions checks the planned partitions and count() for =, in, != and not in filters on a uuid identity partition, and test_identity_transform_column_projection_uuid filters on a uuid identity partition column of a file that does not contain it. Both fail on main and pass with this change. test_scan_prunes_uuid_files_by_bounds checks that the bounds still prune files, test_uuid_expressions_to_pyarrow checks the Arrow filter values, and test_uuid_identity_partition_record_value_and_path in tests/table/test_partitioning.py checks the partition value and path. The tests that pinned the bytes representation now expect a uuid.UUID (tests/expressions/test_literals.py, tests/test_conversions.py and test_determine_partitions_with_uuid_column). The uuid tests also pass with PyArrow 18.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes, worth a note in the changelog. UUIDLiteral now takes a uuid.UUID instead of bytes, and UUIDLiteral.value and from_bytes(UUIDType, ...) return a uuid.UUID; callers that need the encoded value can use .bytes. New uuid identity partition paths use the uuid string, as in Java, instead of base64, and so do the uuid partition bounds in inspect.manifests() and inspect.all_manifests().
This pull request and its description were written by Isaac.
title: Standardize uuid values on uuid.UUID to fix uuid partition filters

body:
Rationale for this change
The row filter parser rejects two kinds of valid numeric literals:
tbl.scan(row_filter="price > 1e-3")
# ParseException: Expected end of text, found 'e'  (at char 9), (line:1, col:10)
tbl.scan(row_filter="quantity in (1, 2.5)")
# ParseException: Expected ')', found '.'  (at char 17), (line:1, col:18)
Decimal literals used pyparsing's common.real(), which has no exponent, so 1e-3 parses as 1 and the rest is left over. A literal set had to be all decimals or all integers, so a list that mixes 1 and 2.5 did not parse either.
This change parses a number with an exponent (1e-3, -1.5E3, 2.5e1) as a DoubleLiteral: in ANSI SQL it is an approximate numeric literal, and Spark, Trino and DuckDB parse it as a double. Numbers without an exponent parse as before (DecimalLiteral or LongLiteral). A literal set can now mix integers, decimals and doubles. Each token is parsed to its own literal type before the existing set deduplication and binding rules apply. To keep long_col = 1e3 working, a DoubleLiteral with a whole value now converts to int and long columns; a fractional value raises, as it does for a DecimalLiteral. Binding to decimal and double columns uses the existing conversions (a double is rounded to the scale of a decimal column). A list that mixes numbers with strings still raises a ParseException (test_in_different_types).
Are these changes tested?
Yes. In tests/expressions/test_parser.py, test_scientific_notation covers exponents on either side of a comparison and in BETWEEN, test_in_mixed_numbers covers mixed IN lists (in both orders) and NOT IN lists, and test_bind_numeric_literals binds exponent forms against decimal, long and double columns, and a mixed integer and double IN list against a long column. In tests/expressions/test_literals.py, test_double_to_integer_and_long_conversion covers the new conversion, and test_invalid_float_conversions no longer expects a DoubleLiteral to reject int and long. The new tests fail on main and pass with this change.
Are there any user-facing changes?

Rationale for this change
A float filter on a wide decimal column raises decimal.InvalidOperation:
# amt is decimal(38, 2)
tbl.scan(row_filter=GreaterThan("amt", 1e26)).to_arrow()
# decimal.InvalidOperation: [<class 'decimal.InvalidOperation'>]

# amt is decimal(38, 30)
tbl.scan(row_filter=LessThan("amt", 0.5)).to_arrow()
# decimal.InvalidOperation: [<class 'decimal.InvalidOperation'>]
FloatLiteral.to(DecimalType) and DoubleLiteral.to(DecimalType) quantize the value to the column's scale under the default decimal context, which keeps 28 digits. When the quantized value has more digits than that (1e26 with 2 decimals, or 0.5 with 30 decimals), quantize raises. A decimal column can hold up to 38 digits, so these are valid filters.
This change quantizes under a local context with enough precision for the result, in one helper used by both conversions. Rounding is unchanged (ROUND_HALF_UP), and positive and negative infinity still raise the ValueError added in #4287 for #4286. NaN remains rejected when a literal is constructed.

body:
Closes #4291.
Rationale for this change
Follow-up to #4292, which handled the rewrite itself. This covers the retry conflict check from the issue.
When a commit retries, _validate_no_new_deletes_for_data_files checks that no new delete file applies to the data files being replaced. It built its delete index with the operation's filter, though, so _filter_manifest_entries skipped any delete file whose column bounds can't match that filter. A partial delete rewrites those data files in full, so a concurrent delete outside the filter went unnoticed. The retry then committed the rewritten file, and the rows that delete removed came back.
Now every delete file added since the starting snapshot is checked against the replaced data files. The filter is no longer used there, so data_filter and case_sensitive are dropped from the private function's signature. _validate_no_new_delete_files, the filter-based check, is unchanged.
Are these changes tested?

a stale table handle starts delete("k = 1");
meanwhile, a position delete storing the row (2, 'b') is committed. It has bounds k = 2, built with commit_partition_position_delete;
the retried delete must raise ValidationException, leaving k = [1, 3].

Without the fix, the test fails with DID NOT RAISE ValidationException, because the retry commits over the concurrent delete.
Are there any user-facing changes?

body:
Closes #3662
Rationale for this change
Every manifest in a table carries the same Avro schema string in its header, but AvroFileHeader.get_schema() parsed and converted that string to an Iceberg Schema on every file open. During scan planning this repeats the same conversion once per manifest.
This caches the conversion by schema string with functools.lru_cache, so each distinct schema is converted once per process.

Schema is a frozen model, so sharing the cached instance between readers is safe.
lru_cache keeps at most 128 schema strings; a process sees only a few distinct manifest schemas.

Builds on #3663 by @vishnuprakaz (picked up with his 👍 on the issue); he is credited as co-author on the commit.
Benchmark
plan_files() on an unpartitioned table with 150 manifests (local SqlCatalog, 7 runs in one process), Python 3.14.7, Apple M5 Pro:

Before
After

Schema conversions in one plan_files()
151
1

plan_files() median
~56 ms
~30 ms

plan_files() first call
~96 ms
~67 ms

Benchmark script
import statistics
import sys
import tempfile
import time

import pyarrow as pa
from pyiceberg.avro.file import AvroSchemaConversion
from pyiceberg.catalog.sql import SqlCatalog

manifests = int(sys.argv[1])
repeats = 7

warehouse = tempfile.mkdtemp()
catalog = SqlCatalog("bench", uri=f"sqlite:///{warehouse}/catalog.db", warehouse=f"file://{warehouse}")
catalog.create_namespace("ns")
table = catalog.create_table("ns.t", schema=pa.schema([("id", pa.int64())]))
for i in range(manifests):
    table.append(pa.table({"id": pa.array([i], pa.int64())}))

calls = 0
original = AvroSchemaConversion.avro_to_iceberg

def counting(self, avro_schema):
    global calls
    calls += 1
    return original(self, avro_schema)

AvroSchemaConversion.avro_to_iceberg = counting

timings = []
for run in range(repeats):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    tasks = list(table.scan().plan_files())
    timings.append((time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000)
    if run == 0:
        first_run_calls = calls

print(f"manifests={manifests} data_files={len(tasks)}")
print(f"conversions: first plan_files={first_run_calls}, all {repeats} runs={calls}")
print(f"plan_files ms: first={timings[0]:.1f} median={statistics.median(timings):.1f} min={min(timings):.1f}")
Run with uv run python bench_plan_files.py 150.

Are these changes tested?
Yes. Added test_get_schema_reuses_conversion_for_identical_schema_strings in tests/avro/test_file.py: it checks the converted schema, that two headers with the same schema string return the same instance, and that a different string returns a different one. The full unit suite passes locally.

body:
Rationale for this change
A case-insensitive lookup on a schema with two columns whose names differ only by case uses the last one. Schema._lazy_name_to_id_lower builds the lower-case index with a dict comprehension, so id overwrites ID, and Schema.find_field and Schema.select use that index for case-insensitive name lookups:
# columns ID (field 1) and id (field 2); rows (ID, id): (5, 7) and (6, 5)
tbl.scan(row_filter=EqualTo("ID", 5), case_sensitive=False).to_arrow()  # returns (6, 5), the row whose id is 5
tbl.delete("ID = 5", case_sensitive=False)  # removes (6, 5); (5, 7) is kept
The same wrong column is used by sort order updates and by schema updates (delete_column("ID") drops id, rename_column("ID", "key") renames id).
Java does not pick a column here. TypeUtil.indexByLowerCaseName throws Cannot build lower case index: ID and id collide, and Schema.caseInsensitiveFindField and SchemaUpdate use that index, so the lookup fails.
This change makes the index raise ValueError: Cannot build lower case index: ID and id collide (the same message as Java) when two different field IDs share a lower-case name. As in Java's Schema lookup, building the lower-case index fails for any requested name when the schema contains a collision, including when the requested name is unambiguous. Names that map to the same field ID, such as the short name of a list element struct field, are not collisions. Case-sensitive lookups do not change. StructType.field_by_name uses a separate lookup and is outside this change, so it remains a divergence from Java: it can still return the first matching field (it serves union_by_name). Java's Types.StructType.caseInsensitiveField builds its index with ImmutableMap.Builder.build(), which throws on duplicate keys, so a case-insensitive unionByNameWith on a struct with ID and id fails in Java. I will follow up with a separate PR for that.
Callers that treated any ValueError from a lookup as "not found" (UpdateSchema.add_column, the move methods, the identifier field check on commit, and the metadata column check in scan projection) now use a private lookup that returns None for a missing name and still raises for an ambiguous one. Without updating the add-column check, an index-only fix would let table.update_schema(case_sensitive=False).add_column("Id", LongType()).commit() add a third case variant.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_case_insensitive_operations_raise_on_case_variant_columns in tests/table/test_init.py runs a delete, a scan, a sort order update, and schema updates with case_sensitive=False on a table with ID and id, for the memory, sql and sql_without_rowcount catalogs. Each must raise, and the table must be unchanged afterwards. It fails on main, where the delete does not raise. test_case_sensitive_and_unambiguous_operations_are_unchanged checks exact-case lookups on the same table and a case-insensitive delete on a table without a collision; it passes on main and with this change. In tests/test_schema.py, test_schema_case_insensitive_lookup_of_case_variant_names_raises and test_schema_case_insensitive_lookup_of_nested_case_variant_names_raises fail on main with DID NOT RAISE, and test_schema_case_insensitive_lookup_of_list_element_struct_field covers the same-ID short names and passes on main and with this change. test_schema_case_insensitive_lookup_rejects_collision_for_any_name, test_metadata_column_projection_propagates_case_collision and test_identifier_field_lookup_propagates_case_collision cover unambiguous and missing names, the metadata column projection and the identifier field check; they fail on main.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes: case-insensitive name lookups through Schema.find_field and Schema.select now raise ValueError when the schema has names that differ only by case, instead of silently using the last column. Case-sensitive lookups are unchanged.
This pull request and its description were written by Isaac.
title: Reject colliding names in case-insensitive Schema lookups

body:
Rationale for this change
Two defaults give ascending sort fields the nulls-last order, which disagrees with Java and with SortField's own default for ascending fields. The same ascending field can therefore be recorded with different null orders depending on how it is built.
Table.update_sort_order().asc(name, transform) with no null_order records nulls-last:
tbl.update_sort_order().asc("user_id", IdentityTransform()).commit()
tbl.sort_order().fields[0].null_order  # NullOrder.NULLS_LAST, expected NULLS_FIRST
SortField built with a str direction also gets nulls-last, while the enum member gets nulls-first:
SortField(source_id=1, transform=IdentityTransform(), direction="asc").null_order  # NULLS_LAST
SortField(source_id=1, transform=IdentityTransform(), direction=SortDirection.ASC).null_order  # NULLS_FIRST
Java's SortOrderBuilder.asc(String) uses NullOrder.NULLS_FIRST (its Javadoc says "ascending with nulls first"), and desc(String) uses NULLS_LAST. SortField picks nulls-first for SortDirection.ASC and nulls-last otherwise. So desc() agrees in all three places, and only the ascending default in UpdateSortOrder.asc() differs. The spec requires null-order in every sort field and does not define a default, so Java and SortField are the reference.
In SortField, the set_null_order validator chooses the default by comparing the raw direction with SortDirection.ASC. SortDirection is a plain Enum, so the str "asc" never matches and gets the descending default. Pydantic converts the value to the enum afterwards, so the field ends up ascending with nulls-last.
This change:

UpdateSortOrder.asc() defaults to NullOrder.NULLS_FIRST. desc() keeps NULLS_LAST.
set_null_order converts the direction to SortDirection before it chooses the default.

An explicit null order is used as given. Existing sort orders are not changed, because their null order is already stored. The asc() default came in with UpdateSortOrder in #2552. Calls that omit null_order now request nulls-first, also on existing tables, where a matching existing sort order may be reused. Pass NullOrder.NULLS_LAST explicitly to keep the previous behaviour.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_update_sort_order_default_null_order in tests/catalog/test_catalog_behaviors.py runs through the catalog fixture (memory, SQL, and SQL without rowcount catalogs). It commits asc() and desc() with no null order and checks the stored sort order, then commits explicit null orders and checks that they are kept. test_deserialize_sort_field_str_direction in tests/table/test_sorting.py checks that "asc" and "desc" validate to the same SortField as the enum members, with the matching default null order. Both fail on main with NullOrder.NULLS_LAST where NullOrder.NULLS_FIRST is expected, and both pass with this change. The integration tests in tests/integration/test_sort_order_update.py pass explicit null orders, so they do not depend on the default.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes. update_sort_order().asc() without a null order now records nulls-first (it recorded nulls-last), and SortField with a str direction now gets the same default as the enum member. Please add the changelog label.
This pull request and its description were written by Isaac.
title: Default ascending sort fields to nulls-first

body:
Rationale for this change
rename_field gives the wrong result when the new name belongs to a void partition field. A void field keeps its name after remove_field on a v1 table. On a v2 table, an explicit void field (add_field with VoidTransform) keeps its name too. Renaming a live field onto that name should give the live field the requested name and move the void field out of the way, as Java does. Instead, the live field is renamed to <old name>_<void field id> and the requested name is dropped:
# v1 table: identity(x) (field id 1000), bucket[16](y) named y_shard (field id 1001)
table.update_spec().remove_field("y_shard").commit()
table.update_spec().rename_field("x", "y_shard").commit()
# before: [(1000, "x_1001", identity), (1001, "y_shard", void)]
# after:  [(1000, "y_shard", identity), (1001, "y_shard_1001", void)]
The cause is the recursive call in UpdateSpec.rename_field. For a void target it called rename_field(name, name + "_" + field_id). That renames the live field and returns, so the requested rename is never recorded. The fix renames the void field to <new name>_<field id> and then records the requested rename. This is the same sequence as BaseUpdatePartitionSpec.renameField in Java. Related: #4307 handles removing and adding a field with the same name in one update; this change handles renaming onto an existing void field's name. add_field also calls rename_field, so nested void-name collisions use the corrected sequence. Field ids, source ids and transforms do not change, only the names do.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. Five tests in tests/table/test_init.py:

test_update_spec_rename_onto_removed_partition_field_name (runs for each catalog fixture variant): a v1 remove_field, then a rename onto the removed name. It reloads the table from the catalog and checks names, field ids, source ids and transforms.
test_update_spec_rename_onto_explicit_void_partition_field_name (v2 table): an explicit void field, then a rename onto its name.
test_update_spec_rename_to_unused_partition_field_name: a control that renames onto an unused name, which must keep working as before.
test_update_spec_rename_onto_void_rejects_removal_in_same_update: checks both operation orders on v1 and v2.
test_update_spec_cascades_void_name_collisions: checks nested void-name collisions through both rename_field and add_field.

Without this change, the two rename tests fail with the live field named x_1001, the removal test fails because nothing is raised, and the cascade test fails on the resulting names. All five tests pass with this change, and the unused-name control passes on both.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes: renaming onto the name of a void partition field now gives that name to the renamed field, and the void field becomes <name>_<field id>. Removing the existing void field and then renaming onto its name in the same update now raises Cannot delete and rename partition field <name>, and the reverse order raises Cannot rename and delete field <name>. Both checks match Java; before, both sequences committed the wrong name for the live field.
This pull request and its description were written by Isaac.
title: Apply rename_field onto the name of a void partition field

body:
Rationale for this change
CPython 3.15 is out (3.15.2), but PyIceberg cannot be installed on it from wheels:

zstandard is a core dependency, and it publishes no cp315 wheel: 0.25.0 (2025-09-14) is still its latest release. Its 3.15 PRs, indygreg/python-zstandard#357 and #372, are open. Without a C compiler, pip install pyiceberg fails on 3.15.
pyiceberg itself ships no cp315 wheel either, because CIBW_PROJECT_REQUIRES_PYTHON stops at <3.15.

Python 3.14 added a zstd module to the standard library: compression.zstd, from PEP 784. PyIceberg only needs one-shot compress and decompress (the Avro codec and Puffin blobs), so on 3.14+ the third-party package is not needed at all.
What changes

pyiceberg/table/puffin.py uses compression.zstd.decompress on Python 3.14+. Below 3.14 it keeps zstandard.ZstdDecompressor().decompress.
pyiceberg/avro/codecs/zstandard_codec.py uses compression.zstd.compress and decompress on 3.14+. Below 3.14 the existing zstandard code is unchanged, only indented under the version check (git diff -w shows the real change).
In pyproject.toml, the dependency becomes zstandard>=0.13.0; python_version < '3.14'. uv.lock is regenerated with uv lock.
The wheel build adds 3.15: CIBW_PROJECT_REQUIRES_PYTHON becomes >=3.11,<3.16, and 3.15 joins the setup-python list. cibuildwheel v4.3.4 already builds cp315 by default.
CIBW_TEST_SKIP: "cp315-*" is set for now. The test step syncs the locked dev group, which pins pyarrow 25.0.1 and numpy 2.4.6 through pyspark[connect], and neither has a cp315 wheel. Moving those pins is a separate change, and the skip can go once it lands.

The version check follows the existing sys.version_info >= (3, 14) pattern (uuid7 in catalog/rest/__init__.py), so mypy checks each branch for the interpreter it runs on.
PEP 784 makes compression.zstd an optional module, built when libzstd is available; python-build-standalone (what uv installs) ships it on 3.14 and 3.15. A CPython built without it fails at import time, as a missing zstandard does today.

Rationale for this change
PyIceberg already models partition statistics in the table metadata: PartitionStatisticsFile, TableMetadata.partition_statistics, and the SetPartitionStatisticsUpdate and RemovePartitionStatisticsUpdate table updates (#2192). Table and Transaction have no builder for these updates; callers currently need to construct the update objects and commit them through the catalog API.
Java has this API. Table.updatePartitionStatistics() and Transaction.updatePartitionStatistics() return an UpdatePartitionStatistics with setPartitionStatistics(file) and removePartitionStatistics(snapshotId) (api/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/UpdatePartitionStatistics.java, core/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/SetPartitionStatistics.java).
This PR adds the same API to PyIceberg:

Table.update_partition_statistics() and Transaction.update_partition_statistics(), next to update_statistics().
UpdatePartitionStatistics in pyiceberg/table/update/partition_statistics.py, modelled on UpdateStatistics. Pending operations are applied on commit, for chained and with block operations alike, with sets applied before removals as in Java.
set_partition_statistics(snapshot_id, statistics_path, file_size_in_bytes) builds the PartitionStatisticsFile and replaces the file already set for that snapshot. It takes the fields rather than the file object, so PartitionStatisticsFile can evolve separately from this API. Java's setPartitionStatistics takes the file object.
remove_partition_statistics(snapshot_id) uses the existing RemovePartitionStatisticsUpdate.

table.update_partition_statistics().set_partition_statistics(
    snapshot_id=snapshot_id, statistics_path="s3://bucket/partition-stats.parquet", file_size_in_bytes=1024
).commit()

with table.update_partition_statistics() as update:
    update.set_partition_statistics(
        snapshot_id=snapshot_id, statistics_path="s3://bucket/partition-stats.parquet", file_size_in_bytes=1024
    )
    update.remove_partition_statistics(other_snapshot_id)
Related open PRs: #4087 fixes UpdateStatistics.remove_statistics, which replaces the pending operations instead of appending to them. This PR does not copy that pattern. #4364 removes partition statistics when their snapshots are removed. This PR changes only the RemovePartitionStatisticsUpdate handler in pyiceberg/table/update/__init__.py, a different part of that file from the snapshot removal handler that #4364 changes, and does not touch the snapshot expiry code. #4364 only removes entries that exist, so the no-op change does not affect its path.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. Four tests in tests/table/test_statistics.py use the catalog fixture (in-memory and SQL catalogs) and go through the public API:

test_update_partition_statistics: set, replace the file for the same snapshot, set in a with block, remove, and reload the table from the catalog.
test_update_partition_statistics_set_and_remove_in_one_update: operations on different snapshots are both applied. On the same snapshot the removal wins in either call order, with or without an existing file. Repeated sets keep the last file, and repeated removals are no-ops.
test_update_partition_statistics_in_transaction: pending changes are visible in transaction.table_metadata, but not in table.metadata or a catalog reload, until the transaction commits. An exception rolls them back.
test_remove_partition_statistics_without_file_is_noop: removing a snapshot without a file, once or repeated, commits and leaves the metadata unchanged.

The low-level handler is covered by test_remove_partition_statistics_update_without_file_is_noop in tests/table/test_init.py.
All four tests fail on main with AttributeError: the transaction test reports that Transaction has no update_partition_statistics attribute, and the other three report the missing attribute on Table. All four pass with this change. The low-level test in tests/table/test_init.py fails on main with ValueError and passes with this change. I also chec […]

body:
Rationale for this change
write.metadata.compression-codec has no effect on the metadata file name. With write.metadata.compression-codec=gzip, PyIceberg still writes 00000-<uuid>.metadata.json, while Java writes 00000-<uuid>.gz.metadata.json and gzips the file. The gzip reader and writer already choose gzip from the .gz.metadata.json suffix (added in apache/iceberg#7984), so only the file name is missing.
The Java reference is BaseMetastoreTableOperations.newTableMetadataFilePath. It reads write.metadata.compression-codec (default none) from the metadata being written, and TableMetadataParser.getFileExtension returns .gz.metadata.json for gzip and .metadata.json for none. Codec.fromName accepts the names case-insensitively and throws for any other value.
This PR does the same in LocationProvider.new_table_metadata_file_location, the one place PyIceberg builds table metadata file names. The codec is read from the table properties. none (the default) keeps .metadata.json, gzip gives .gz.metadata.json, and any other value raises ValueError when a metadata file is written. The codec names and their suffixes are defined in pyiceberg/serializers.py, next to the reader's GZIP constant. The metastore catalogs use this for every metadata file they create or commit: SQL, in-memory, Hive, Glue, DynamoDB and BigQuery on create, and SQL, in-memory, Hive and Glue on commit (DynamoDB and BigQuery do not implement commit yet). The codec comes from the properties of the metadata being written, so a commit that sets it applies to the file that commit writes. The new TableProperties.METADATA_COMPRESSION constant is documented in mkdocs/docs/configuration.md.
from pyiceberg.table import TableProperties

table = catalog.create_table(
    "db.events",
    schema=schema,
    properties={TableProperties.METADATA_COMPRESSION: "gzip"},
)
table.metadata_location  # .../metadata/00000-<uuid>.gz.metadata.json
PyIceberg's REST client is unchanged: the REST server writes the table metadata files, so whether they are compressed is up to the server.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. Four new tests in tests/catalog/test_catalog_behaviors.py run on the in-memory and SQL catalogs, each with the three identifier shapes:

test_table_writes_gzip_metadata_when_compression_codec_is_set: the file name ends with .gz.metadata.json and the content starts with the gzip magic bytes. A later append keeps the codec and the version parses from the gzip name (00001-), and load_table returns the same metadata.
test_table_metadata_compression_codec_default_and_set_on_commit: a table with the default still writes .metadata.json. A commit that sets gzip makes the next metadata file a .gz.metadata.json.
test_table_metadata_invalid_compression_codec_raises: snappy raises ValueError on create, and no table is created. On commit it raises and the table is unchanged.
test_table_metadata_legacy_invalid_compression_codec_on_commit: a table registered with snappy keeps its metadata location on a commit with no changes. A commit that changes something raises ValueError and leaves the table unchanged, and removing the property commits normally.

tests/table/test_locations.py adds test_new_table_metadata_file_location_compression_codec (none, NONE, gzip and GZIP) and test_new_table_metadata_file_location_invalid_compression_codec.
The added catalog tests cover in-memory, SQL, and SQL without row-count support. Hive, Glue, DynamoDB and BigQuery share the filename generator; this PR adds no codec-specific tests to their existing unit suites, which use mocked services.
These fail on main. Run against main with only the new TableProperties constant added, the gzip and default tests fail with AssertionError (the file name does not end with .gz.metadata.json), and the invalid-codec and legacy-codec tests fail with DID NOT RAISE ValueError. They pass with this change. The unit suite has no new failures.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes. With write.metadata.compression-codec=gzip, new table meta […]

Closes #4399
Rationale for this change
A scan whose row_filter tests a list or map column for null (tags is null, props is not null) fails in to_arrow() with ValueError: Cannot explicitly project List or Map types.
ArrowScan._projected_field_ids leaves list and map IDs out of the projected schema's IDs, because prune_columns rebuilds those columns from their nested fields, but it adds the filter's field IDs as they are. A null test on a list or map column adds the column's own ID, and prune_columns rejects it. This change projects the nested fields of such a column instead, the same way a selected list or map column is read.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_projection_null_filter_on_list_and_map in tests/io/test_pyarrow.py runs IsNull and NotNull on a list, a map and a list of structs, with the column selected and with only id selected. It fails on main with the ValueError above and passes with this change.
Ran locally: pytest tests/io/test_pyarrow.py -m unit, and the ruff, ruff-format and mypy hooks on the two changed files. The rest of the suite and the integration tests are left to CI.
Are there any user-facing changes?
IS NULL and IS NOT NULL filters on list and map columns return the matching rows instead of raising.

body:
Summary
Data files written by the PyArrow writer always had an empty nan_value_counts map, because the counts were never computed. The scan planner supports NaN counts, so files written by pyiceberg could never be pruned on is_nan, not_nan, or range filters, while files written by parquet-mr could.
Changes

Count the non-null NaNs of the top-level float and double columns from the Arrow table the writer receives, since PyArrow does not expose a NaN count on its Parquet column statistics.
Accumulate the counts across batches and pass them into data_file_statistics_from_parquet_metadata, so all the statistics logic stays in one place.
Skip columns whose metrics mode is none, like the value and null counts, and compute the statistics plan once per writer.
Leave a column out of the map when it cannot be counted, which only means the file cannot be pruned on NaN counts.

Nested float and double columns are not counted yet; that needs flattening through lists, structs, and maps and can follow separately.
The parquet_file_to_data_file (add_files) path still reports empty NaN counts, since PyArrow does not expose a NaN count in the Parquet column statistics. That path needs a separate change, so #4396 stays open.
Testing

Added a test asserting the NaN counts of a written file, and one asserting d IS NAN now prunes a file without NaNs.
Added tests for counts accumulated across multiple write() calls, for a column with metrics mode none, and for metrics mode none as the default.
Updated the merge manifests integration test for the NaN counts on written files.
make test passes (4697 passed, 5 skipped).

Part of #4396.
title: Report NaN value counts for written Parquet files

Summary
PyIceberg never wrote Parquet page indexes, so readers that support them cannot skip non-matching pages during predicate evaluation. PyArrow already supports this with ParquetWriter(write_page_index=True), and the Java writer writes these indexes by default, so PyIceberg now does the same.
Changes

Write Parquet column and offset indexes by default, matching the Java writer.
Add the write.parquet.page-index-enabled table property, default true, as an opt-out.
Document the property in the write options table.
Update the expected column sizes in the manifest merge integration test, since files written with page indexes have different column chunk sizes.

Testing

Added a test that writes with the property defaulting to on and explicitly set to false, and checks has_column_index and has_offset_index on the resulting row group.
Unit tests, lint, and integration tests run in CI.

Closes #3847
title: Write Parquet page indexes by default

body:
Summary
Filtered scans raised or returned wrong rows at two kinds of edge values.

Year and month partitions raised OverflowError when a filter projected past 9999-12-31 or before 0001-01-01, because the transform converted the day count to a datetime.date. 9999-12-31 is a common "no end date" value.
EqualTo, In, NotEqualTo, and the range comparisons (<, <=, >, >=) on inf returned wrong rows for float columns. A Python float becomes a DoubleLiteral, and converting that to a float column turned inf into FloatAboveMax or FloatBelowMin, which bound the predicate to AlwaysFalse or AlwaysTrue.

Changes

Compute years and months from a day count with integer arithmetic, so a projection just past the last representable date yields year 10000 and matches no partition instead of raising. Results inside the representable range are unchanged.
Convert inf and -inf to a FloatLiteral for float columns, like any other float that fits. For float columns this also changes how the range comparisons bind: < and <= with inf no longer match every row, and > and >= with -inf no longer match every row. For example, table.delete(LessThan("x", math.inf)) used to delete every row, including the inf, NaN and null rows, and now leaves exactly those rows.

Notes

Iceberg-Java applies the same range check in DoubleLiteral.to(FLOAT), so Java binds float_col = <double infinity> to alwaysFalse. This change intentionally diverges from that.
StringLiteral.to(FloatType) still turns values such as "Infinity" into FloatAboveMax, so EqualTo("x", "Infinity") returns no rows. That is the same bug through the string path and is left for a follow-up.

Testing

Added unit tests for the day and microsecond conversions at and beyond the date range, the year projection at both date limits, and the infinity literal conversion.
Added scan and delete tests for inf, In and the range comparisons on a float column, and a year-partitioned table scanned at 9999-12-31.
tests/utils/test_datetime.py, tests/expressions/test_literals.py, tests/expressions/test_projection.py and the non-cloud tests in tests/io/test_pyarrow.py pass (493 passed, 1 skipped).

Closes #4404
title: Fix scan filters at the edges of the date and float ranges

body:
Summary
The writer, like Java, truncates with two's complement arithmetic, so values from the minimum of the type wrap to a partition value at the top of the range. The Python transform did not wrap, so scan planning projected a different partition, pruned the file, and lost those rows for EqualTo and In.
Changes

Wrap the Python truncate transform into the range of the source type, which fixes EqualTo and In.
Return no strict projection for int and long truncate ranges that can match the wrapped partition, because it does not sort with the other partition values. The residual evaluator then keeps the original predicate, so count() reads the file instead of trusting its record count.

The writer output is unchanged, matching Java and existing tables. This also fixes add_files for a Parquet file whose minimum is the type minimum: on main, adding the file raised struct.error: 'i' format requires -2147483648 <= number <= 2147483647; the file now gets the partition value the writer uses.
Range filters keep Java's projection. ProjectionUtil.truncateInteger does not add the wrapped partition for < and >, so those filters can still miss rows near the minimum. That gap belongs in the reference implementation first and is tracked in apache/iceberg#19075.
Testing

Added tests for the transform at the type minimum and the projection at the type minimum.
Added an end-to-end scan of a truncate[1000] int partition with EqualTo at the minimum.
Added count() coverage on a table with write.metadata.metrics.default=counts, where there are no column bounds.
tests/expressions/test_projection.py and tests/test_transforms.py pass (319 tests), along with the new scan tests. The wide tests/io/test_pyarrow.py run had only the GCS and ADLS tests failing for missing credentials.

Part of #4403
title: Keep rows in truncate partitions near the minimum int or long

body:
Rationale for this change
Iceberg v3 allows date to be promoted to timestamp and timestamp_ns. The promotion does not rewrite the
bounds of existing data files, so a bound written before the promotion is still a 4-byte day count from
1970-01-01. The spec says readers must infer the write-time type from the length of the bound: in the
"Schema Evolution" section of format/spec.md, a 4-byte timestamp or timestamp_ns bound is a date.
from_bytes registers TimestampType and TimestampNanoType with the 8-byte decoder, so such a bound fails:
from pyiceberg.conversions import from_bytes, to_bytes
from pyiceberg.types import DateType, TimestampType

from_bytes(TimestampType(), to_bytes(DateType(), 18793))  # 2021-06-15
# on main: struct.error: unpack requires a buffer of 8 bytes
# with this change: 1623715200000000
On a v3 table with retained date bounds after promotion to timestamp, tbl.scan(row_filter=GreaterThan("d", "2022-01-01T00:00:00")).plan_files() raises this struct.error when evaluating those bounds. tbl.inspect.files() raises it after promotion to either timestamp or timestamp_ns.
The fix decodes a 4-byte bound of TimestampType and TimestampNanoType as a signed day count, scaled to microseconds (x 86,400,000,000) or nanoseconds (x 86,400,000,000,000), and returns the exact Python int. The 8-byte path is unchanged. The fallback decodes 4-byte bounds; unsupported lengths still raise struct.error. The change adds no per-file containers or caches. TimeType, TimestamptzType and TimestamptzNanoType keep their decoder, because the spec does not allow date to be promoted to them. The fix is in from_bytes, the one decoder that the inclusive and strict metrics evaluators and inspect all use, so no call site changes.
Planning compares such bounds exactly, because Python ints have no int64 limit. Metadata tables are different: converting a bound outside the Arrow range to a timestamp raises OverflowError. For date bounds promoted to timestamp_ns, representable midnight dates run from 1677-09-22 through 2262-04-11 inclusive; metadata inspection raises OverflowError for dates outside that interval. The spec's runtime failure rule (Schema Evolution) applies to promoted data values. It does not apply to bounds, because the bounds rules only require a lower bound at or below all values and an upper bound at or above all values, so a bound can be wider than the data (format/spec.md, the data file fields lower_bounds and upper_bounds). An out-of-range bound therefore does not show that a data value overflows.
This PR follows the spec rather than Java. Java's Conversions.fromByteBuffer
(api/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/types/Conversions.java, lines 171-179) returns the raw day count for a
4-byte TIMESTAMP or TIMESTAMP_NANO bound without scaling it. Comparing that count with a microsecond literal
could prune a file that has matching rows.
Alternatives considered: B, raise ValueError for bounds that do not fit in int64. That fails planning or inspection even when every row is representable, because a bound need not occur in the data. C, treat such bounds as unknown, or leave them unavailable in metadata tables. That avoids the errors, but it changes the evaluator and metadata contracts, so it is left for a follow-up. Actual-value overflow checks belong to date-promotion support.
This extends #3293, which added the same kind of 4-byte fallback for int to long and float to double bounds, and #4314, which added the inspect test for those types (it closes #3744). Neither covers date to timestamp.
Out of scope: normal schema promotion and reading date data files as timestamps remain unsupported (related closed PR #2586). Comparison filters on timestamp_ns remain unsupported for string, integer and datetime literals (#4078).
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_from_bytes_date_bound_promoted_to_timestamp in tests/test_conversions.py checks exact micros and nanos for 4-byte day counts, including a date before 1970, and checks that the 8-byte encoding i […]
title: Decode 4-byte bounds of date columns promoted to timestamp

promote() allows three type changes that aren't valid promotions in the spec: string -> binary, binary -> string and fixed(16) -> uuid. update_column() and union_by_name() use promote(), so schema updates allow them too. That's on purpose (string <-> binary was discussed in apache/iceberg#5151, and fixed(16) -> uuid is there because older PyArrow versions had no UUID type), but the code didn't say so.
This PR adds comments for these edge cases in promote() and next to its use in update_column(). No behavior change.

Yes, added test_update_column_allows_non_spec_promotions in tests/test_schema.py. It checks that update_column() allows the three changes and still rejects fixed(15) -> uuid. test_promotion already covers promote() itself.
Are there any user-facing changes?
No.

body:
Rationale for this change
A position delete file can list rows of several data files. ArrowScan loads the position deletes of every task and
merges them into one map keyed by data file path. A data file then gets the positions of any delete file that names
its path, even when the planner did not attach that delete file to its task. So a delete file that also names another
data file can remove rows from a file it was not planned for, undoing the sequence number and partition checks that
DeleteFileIndex made for it.
The trigger, on a v2 table with a position delete file written by another engine. P has ids 0..9, Q has ids 100..109,
and the delete file, committed before the first line, lists row 0 of P and row 0 of Q:
tbl.delete("id < 10")                       # removes P as a whole file
tbl.add_files([p_path])                     # registers P again, so its data sequence number is newer than the delete's
tbl.scan().to_arrow()                       # 18 rows, id 0 missing; expected 0..9 and 101..109
tbl.scan().count()                          # 19
tbl.scan(row_filter="id < 10").to_arrow()   # 0..9, but the unfiltered scan restricted to id < 10 gives 1..9
The delete predates P, so P must keep its row 0. Scan Planning in format/spec.md says that a position delete applies
only when "The data file's data sequence number is less than or equal to the delete file's data sequence number", and
that the data file and position delete file must have equal partitions (both spec and partition values). Java gives each task only its
own deletes: GenericDeleteFilter is built from task.deletes(), and BaseDeleteLoader reads the delete files it is
given and keeps the positions for the data file path it is asked for.
This change keeps, for each delete file, only the positions of the data files whose task has that delete file attached
(task.delete_files). Each delete file is still read once, and the key is unchanged: the path plus the content offset
and size, so deletion vector ranges in one Puffin file stay separate. The root cause is in the loader, which drops the
association between a delete file and its task, so the lookup in _record_batches_from_scan_tasks_and_deletes is left
as it is. Planning is unchanged; the read path adds one set entry per delete file and task.
_DeleteFileKey comes from #3478. PR #3285 also edits _read_all_delete_files (it skips non-position delete files in
the inner loop over task.delete_files). The two changes merge cleanly, and the merged function keeps both.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. Both new tests fail on main and pass with this change.

test_position_delete_respects_sequence_number_of_readded_file (tests/table/test_init.py, catalog fixture) runs the
trigger above, and a second shape where the delete is committed after P is registered again, so it removes row 0 of
both files. It asserts the exact rows, that count() agrees with to_arrow(), and that the row-filtered scan agrees
with the unfiltered scan. On main, the first shape fails because id 0 is missing.
test_read_all_delete_files_only_loads_positions_for_tasks_it_is_attached_to (tests/io/test_pyarrow.py) checks the
loader output for three attachment shapes. The third gives the first data file a newer delete file as well, so a fix
that merges the positions of all tasks also fails it.

commit_partition_position_delete (tests/table/test_commit_retry.py) now takes a list of (file_path, pos) rows, so one
delete file can name two data files. Its existing callers pass one row.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes, a read bug fix: scans no longer drop rows that a newer data file keeps, and an upsert over such a file no longer
inserts a duplicate of a row it should update. There is no API change.
Please add the changelog label.
This pull request and its description were written by Isaac.
title: Only apply position deletes to the data files they are attached to

body:
What's changed
Implements design A from #4396: data_file_statistics_from_parquet_metadata returned an empty nan_value_counts dict unconditionally, so data files written by the pyarrow writer never reported NaN counts — and NaN-aware scan pruning stayed silently unavailable for them (_InclusiveMetricsEvaluator degrades to ROWS_MIGHT_MATCH without nan counts, for is_nan, not_nan and range predicates via _contains_nans_only).
pyarrow's statistics API does not expose NaN counts (checked on 26.0.1 — no nan_count/has_nan_count), so the writer now counts them from the written table itself:

ParquetFormatWriter.write() accumulates pa.compute.is_nan(...) sums per top-level float/double field (is_nan is null on nulls and sum skips nulls — matching the spec's NaN-count semantics of counting non-null NaN values)
the counts flow through a new optional table_nan_value_counts parameter of data_file_statistics_from_parquet_metadata
the metadata-only caller (parquet_file_to_data_file, used by add_files) keeps its previous behavior — no NaN counts from metadata-only input

Nested float fields keep the previous (empty) behavior for now; the metrics plan and evaluator keys make them a natural follow-up once the top-level path is settled.
Test
test_nan_value_counts_are_written (mixed values + null) and test_nan_value_counts_are_written_across_row_groups (all-NaN, two write() calls) — both verified failing-first on main (nan_value_counts == {}) and passing with the change; the second also pins the pruning win (not_nan now prunes an all-NaN file via _contains_nans_only). Full tests/io/test_pyarrow_stats.py (22) green; the pre-existing azure-fixture failures in test_pyarrow.py are unrelated (missing optional dep in this environment).
AI disclosure: drafted with AI assistance, verified locally by running the failing-first cycle.

Closes #4417
Rationale for this change
pyarrow_to_schema only used field IDs when every column had one (_HasIds used all). If any column lacked an ID, it ignored all IDs and fell back to the name mapping. That fails when physical names differ from the mapped names, which is what happens with Databricks UniForm files that attach IDs to data columns but not to row-tracking columns.
Java's reader treats a file as having IDs if any column has one (ParquetSchemaUtil.hasIds) and ignores the columns without one. This PR does the same, but only when reading data files.
pyarrow_to_schema gets a prune_fields_without_ids flag (default False), set only in _task_to_record_batches. When it's on, fields without an ID are dropped from the Arrow schema before it's converted, so an unsupported type in such a column (e.g. time32[ms]) doesn't break the read. A list whose element has no ID, and a map whose key or value has no ID, is dropped as a whole, since it can't be represented without it. If nothing has an ID, it still falls back to the name mapping as before.
_HasIds and _ConvertToIceberg are unchanged, so the write path keeps the old rule: an append with an extra column that has no ID is still rejected ("PyArrow table contains more columns") instead of silently dropping it.
Are these changes tested?
Yes, in tests/io/test_pyarrow_visitor.py:

the issue's example, with and without a name mapping
partial IDs without pruning still fall back to the name mapping (write path behavior)
a time32[ms] column without an ID is pruned before conversion
nested: a map missing child IDs is dropped, a struct keeps only the children with IDs
list element ID guard, and map key-only / value-only ID guards (the whole map is dropped)
no IDs at all still uses the name mapping

And in tests/io/test_pyarrow.py:

test_projection_partial_field_ids writes a Parquet file with one ID'd column and one ID-less time32[ms] column and reads it through ArrowScan
test_schema_mismatch_additional_field_without_id checks an append with an extra ID-less column is still rejected

make lint passed. pytest tests/ -m unit --ignore=tests/integration passed apart from 60 failures that fail the same way on main here (missing optional deps like pyiceberg-core, thrift, datafusion).
Are there any user-facing changes?
Reading files with IDs on only some columns now works by ID, and columns without IDs are ignored, even if a name mapping is present. Files with IDs on every column, or on none, are read as before. Writes are unchanged.
Limitations

On read, pruned columns are skipped silently (same as Java). They'd only be visible through the name mapping, which isn't used once the file has IDs.
A map with an ID only on its key (or only on its value) is dropped entirely on read rather than partially kept. On write it is still rejected as before.
A struct whose children all lack IDs is dropped too, even if the struct itself has one.

Happy to adjust the approach if you'd prefer something else.
title: Use field IDs when any Parquet column has one and prune the rest

body:
Rationale for this change
Table.append accepts any Arrow column that converts to the Iceberg column type, but the partition transforms of pyiceberg-core only handle the Arrow type that matches the Iceberg type exactly. On a partitioned table these appends fail with a ValueError from pyiceberg-core (FeatureUnsupported => Unsupported data type for bucket transform or Unexpected => Should not call internally for unsupported data type), although the same data appends fine to an unpartitioned table or an identity-partitioned one.
This is easy to hit: pyarrow.csv.read_csv and pyarrow.json.read_json infer timestamp[s], which breaks the common spec of a table partitioned by day on the event time. DuckDB TIMESTAMP_S, TIMESTAMP_MS and SMALLINT come out as timestamp[s], timestamp[ms] and int16, and polars produces large_binary.
import pyarrow as pa
from pyiceberg.catalog.sql import SqlCatalog
from pyiceberg.partitioning import PartitionField, PartitionSpec
from pyiceberg.schema import Schema
from pyiceberg.transforms import DayTransform
from pyiceberg.types import NestedField, TimestampType

catalog = SqlCatalog("c", uri="sqlite:///:memory:", warehouse="file:///tmp/wh")
catalog.create_namespace("n")
schema = Schema(NestedField(1, "ts", TimestampType(), required=False))
spec = PartitionSpec(PartitionField(1, 1000, DayTransform(), "ts_day"))
table = catalog.create_table("n.t", schema, partition_spec=spec)
table.append(pa.table({"ts": pa.array([1, 2], pa.timestamp("s"))}))
# ValueError: Unexpected => Should not call internally for unsupported data type Timestamp(Second, None)
The other affected combinations of Arrow type and transform:

int8, int16, uint8, uint16 (and uint32 or in-range uint64 on a long column) for bucket and truncate
timestamp[s] and timestamp[ms], with or without a time zone, for bucket, day and hour, and for identity with time zone +00:00
large_binary and binary_view for truncate

The fix
_determine_partitions now casts the source column of each partition field to the Arrow type of its Iceberg type (int32/int64, microsecond timestamps, binary) before applying the transform. Only the partition computation changes; the data that is written is unchanged (narrow integers are already widened on write since #2799). large_binary is cast to binary for truncate only (apache/iceberg-rust#3119 tracks LargeBinary support in the Rust truncate kernel), so bucket and identity on large_binary behave as before. Nanosecond timestamps and dictionary-encoded columns are left alone (#4340 covers dictionary).
Partition values are computed on the Iceberg-typed value (the spec hashes int as long, and timestamps are microseconds), which are the values Java computes; the unit test checks every value against the Python transforms.
Are these changes tested?
Yes, in tests/io/test_pyarrow.py:

test_determine_partitions_with_arrow_types_narrower_than_the_iceberg_type checks the partition values of each type and transform pair against the Python transforms
test_determine_partitions_keeps_large_binary_for_bucket checks that bucket on large_binary is not cast
test_append_arrow_types_narrower_than_the_iceberg_type_to_partitioned_table appends to a table partitioned by bucket, day and truncate and checks the scan round trip

The first and the last fail on main (Unsupported data type for bucket transform: Int16) and pass now. pytest tests/io/test_pyarrow.py tests/table/test_partitioning.py tests/test_transforms.py (without the network-bound S3/GCS/ADLS/retry/ssl tests): 557 passed, 1 skipped.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Partitioned tables accept these Arrow column types on append and overwrite.
Behaviour note: an int64 or uint64 Arrow column with values outside the range of an int source column now raises ArrowInvalid (a ValueError subclass) from the cast in _cast_to_transform_input_type.
title: Fix partitioned appends of narrow integer, s/ms timestamp and large_binary columns

Rationale for this change
Follow-up to #4389.
Bug: StructType.field_by_name(name, case_sensitive=False) returns the first match when a struct has two fields that differ only by case, like ID and id. So a case-insensitive union_by_name can silently pick the wrong column:

body:
Closes #4428
Rationale for this change
#4310 sends Idempotency-Key on mutations and lets rest.client.* retry keyed POSTs, but it never looks at the idempotency-key-lifetime the server returns from /v1/config beyond checking it's there. urllib3 sleeps for the full Retry-After (and backoff can add up too), so a retry can go out after the key has expired, and the server may then apply the same mutation twice. The spec says clients SHOULD NOT reuse a key after that window.
This follows what the Java client does (HTTPClient.parseKeyLifetime + ExponentialHttpRequestRetryStrategy, apache/iceberg#18070):

idempotency-key-lifetime is parsed as an ISO-8601 duration (TypeAdapter(timedelta)).

malformed: log a warning and don't bound retries; the key is still sent (same as Java)
zero or negative: keyed requests are never retried

_RetryTimeoutHTTPAdapter.send records a deadline (now + lifetime, monotonic clock) in a ContextVar when the request carries an Idempotency-Key.
A small Retry subclass checks it in increment: if now + next_sleep >= deadline the retry is declined. next_sleep is what Retry.sleep would wait: Retry-After when urllib3 would honor it, otherwise the backoff plus the max jitter.
A declined retry raises MaxRetryError, i.e. it behaves exactly like running out of retries: with raise_on_status=False urllib3 hands back the last response, so _handle_non_200_response still raises the typed error (e.g. ServiceUnavailableError); a connection error is re-raised as before.

Requests without a key (all GET/HEAD, and everything when the server doesn't advertise a lifetime) are untouched.
Are these changes tested?
Yes, in tests/catalog/test_rest.py, using the existing loopback server (now with an optional Retry-After header):

Retry-After: 60 with PT30S lifetime: no retry, ServiceUnavailableError, 1 call
backoff alone exceeding the lifetime (PT5S, factor 10): stops before the second retry
Retry-After: 0 within PT30M: still retried and succeeds
PT0S and -PT5M: keyed POST never retried, key still sent
PT0S doesn't affect unkeyed GETs, they still retry
malformed lifetime: warning logged, keyed POST still retried with the same key
_parse_idempotency_key_lifetime unit cases

make lint passes. pytest tests/catalog -m unit passes except 4 kerberos tests in test_hive.py that fail the same way on main here (kerberos extra not installed locally).
Are there any user-facing changes?
Only for catalogs whose server advertises idempotency-key-lifetime and that set rest.client.max-retries: a keyed mutation is no longer retried once the next attempt would land outside the key's lifetime; the error that would have been raised after exhausting retries is raised earlier instead.
Limitations

The deadline starts when the adapter sends the first attempt, not when the caller started the operation (e.g. the commit retry loop in table/update creates a new key per attempt, so that's fine).
The SigV4 adapter mounted on the catalog URI has its own plain integer retries and doesn't retry POST on status codes, so it isn't changed here.
The lifetime is checked before sleeping, so a slow next attempt itself (e.g. a long socket timeout) can still finish after the window. Java has the same behavior.

#4310 cc @YuangGao. Happy to adjust if u'd prefer a different shape (e.g. doing this in the adapter instead of a Retry subclass). thx!
title: Bound Idempotency-Key retries by the advertised idempotency-key-lifetime

Rationale for this change
Bug: an identity partition on a double or float column writes each NaN row into every NaN partition file when the NaNs differ in the sign bit. float("nan") has the sign bit clear and 0.0 * float("inf") has it set on x86. _determine_partitions groups by the raw bits, so these are two partitions. Each one selects its rows with is_nan, which matches every NaN row:
# table partitioned by identity(value), value is a double
tbl.append(pa.table({"id": [1, 2, 3], "value": [float("nan"), 0.0 * float("inf"), 1.5]}))
sorted(tbl.scan().to_arrow()["id"].to_pylist())  # [1, 1, 2, 2, 3], expected [1, 2, 3]
Fix: canonicalize NaN in the partition helper column before the group by, so every NaN is one partition value, as the spec defines partition equality (Scan Planning). The data column keeps its bits.
Java: Spark computes each row's PartitionKey, then FanoutWriter and ClusteredWriter use Comparators.forType to group all NaNs together. This PR gives _determine_partitions, shared by append and rewrites, the same grouping.
Remaining differences from Java:

-0.0 and 0.0 have the same duplication. #4274 fixes that in _partition_value_filter, and this PR leaves that function alone.
The partition value written is the canonical NaN. Java keeps the NaN of the first row. Both are equal under the spec.

Rationale for this change
Bug: appending a fixed-size list of structs fails. The struct branch of ArrowProjectionVisitor.list rebuilds the list from its first two buffers, which are the validity and offsets buffers only for a variable-size list. A FixedSizeListArray has no offsets buffer, so the rebuilt array is invalid:
import pyarrow as pa

t = pa.table({"v": pa.array([[{"a": 1}, {"a": 2}]], pa.list_(pa.struct([("a", pa.int32())]), 2))})
catalog.create_table("db.t", schema=t.schema).append(t)

Fixes #4438
Rationale for this change
When a scan projects _row_id and has a row filter, _task_to_record_batches adds a temporary column of row positions to each batch. That column always gets the fixed name _POSITION_COLUMN (__iceberg_file_position). If the data file already has a column with that name, the table ends up with two fields of the same name. The lookup then fails with KeyError: 'Field "__iceberg_file_position" exists 2 times in schema'.
The fix picks a free name for the temporary column by putting _ in front until no data column has that name. _determine_partitions already avoids clashes with its _partition_<name> columns this way. body:
Closes #4441
Rationale for this change
FloatLiteral.to(DecimalType) and DoubleLiteral.to(DecimalType) used Decimal(self.value), which takes the exact binary value of the float. For values like 2.675 that value is 2.67499999..., so ROUND_HALF_UP rounded down: literal(2.675).to(DecimalType(10, 2)) gave 2.67 instead of 2.68. This also changed the bound literal of filters on decimal columns, e.g. EqualTo("price", 2.675) bound to 2.67.
This now uses Decimal(str(self.value)), the shortest decimal that round-trips to the float. That matches Java, which uses BigDecimal.valueOf(value).setScale(scale, RoundingMode.HALF_UP).
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_float_and_double_to_decimal_round_half_up_on_shortest_repr in tests/expressions/test_literals.py covers 2.675, 1.005 and -2.675 (which round the wrong way on main), plus 0.125 and 2.674 as controls, for both FloatLiteral and DoubleLiteral. The three wrong cases fail on main and pass with this change. All tests in tests/expressions and tests/test_conversions.py pass.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes. Float and double values converted to a decimal type (for example in filters on decimal columns) now round like Java, Spark and Postgres: 2.675 becomes 2.68.

PartitionSpec.partition_to_path URL-encodes field names and values to match Java, which uses java.net.URLEncoder (PartitionSpec.java). quote_plus differs from it on two characters: Java leaves * as is and escapes ~ to %7E, while PyIceberg wrote %2A and a literal ~. A partition value such as a*b~c therefore got the path a%2Ab~c from PyIceberg and a*b%7Ec from Java, and a different partitions.<path> key in the snapshot summary.

body:
Rationale for this change
A transaction can register a producer that stages no snapshot, for example the delete half of an overwrite on an empty table. _attempt_landed() required a snapshot for every producer, so a commit that landed and was reported as failed was never detected. The retry then raised a validation error and deleted the manifest list and manifests of the snapshot that had already landed, leaving the table unreadable.
Check the snapshot ids in the transaction's AddSnapshotUpdates instead. Those are the snapshots the attempt actually tried to add.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. Two cases in tests/table/test_commit_retry.py simulate a lost response for an overwrite on an empty table, with the default retry budget and with zero retries. Both fail before the change and pass after it. tests/table passes.

body:
Rationale for this change
Arrow table writes ignored the table sort order and always wrote sort_order_id=None, so manifests disagreed with the table metadata and readers could not prune on sort order.
Sort materialized Arrow tables when every sort field uses an identity transform, the column exists at the top level, and all fields agree on null placement. Unpartitioned tables are sorted before bin packing and each partition is sorted on its own. The table sort order id is written on each data file.
Unsupported cases (non-identity transforms, nested or missing columns, mixed null placement, streaming RecordBatchReader writes) keep writing unsorted files and emit a warning.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. New tests in tests/io/test_pyarrow.py cover the four direction and null-placement combinations, the unsupported cases, sorted files per partition, and the streaming warning. tests/table and the local write tests pass.

PyIceberg defaulted to fast append, which adds manifest metadata on every commit. The devlist discussion concluded that merge append is the better default for metadata management, and the earlier change was intentionally deferred until after the 0.12 release.

body:
Rationale for this change
Upsert compared every non-key column to decide whether a matched row changed. For wide or nested rows this is expensive, and callers often already know which column signals a change, such as a hash column.
Add an optional difference_cols parameter to Table.upsert, Transaction.upsert, and get_rows_to_update. When set, only those columns are compared. Unknown columns raise a ValueError, and the selection must contain at least one non-key column.
The parameter is added at the end of the signature to keep positional calls working.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. Unit tests cover comparing only the selected columns, unchanged selected columns, unknown columns, and key-only selections. An end-to-end upsert test confirms that a change in an unselected column does not update the row. tests/table passes.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes. upsert accepts a new optional difference_cols argument.

body:
Rationale for this change
Bug: when every field of an Arrow table carries a field ID, append drops the columns whose field ID is not in the table schema, without an error:
schema = Schema(NestedField(1, "id", LongType()), NestedField(2, "x", LongType()))
tbl = catalog.create_table("db.t", schema=schema)
with_z = Schema(*schema.fields, NestedField(99, "z", LongType()))
tbl.append(pa.Table.from_pylist([{"id": 1, "x": 2, "z": 3}], schema=with_z.as_arrow()))
tbl.scan().to_arrow().to_pylist()
# [{'id': 1, 'x': 2}]
The same happens to a column that was dropped and added back: an Arrow schema taken before delete_column("x") and add_column("x", LongType()) has x with field ID 2, the new x has field ID 3, and the appended values are stored as null. overwrite and dynamic_partition_overwrite lose these columns too, and upsert can lose them on inserts or when updating with a stale ID. Without field IDs, the extra z is already rejected (PyArrow table contains more columns: z). Fokko raised the same concern on #4419 (review): silently dropping a column on append loses data without any signal.
Fix: the four write paths now reject input field IDs that are not in the table schema, before anything is written:
ValueError: PyArrow table contains columns whose field IDs are not in the table schema: z (field ID 99).

add_files is unchanged (#4359). Note that #4444 currently tests that upsert accepts such a stale ID; with this change it raises.
Java: Spark's write builder gives the input the table's field IDs by name (SparkSchemaUtil.convert -> TypeUtil.reassignIds) and fails on unknown columns (Field z not found in source schema) unless merge-schema adds them first. PyIceberg has no merge-schema option on write and keeps the input's own IDs when every field has one, so it rejects the stale x instead of writing it to the new x.
Are these changes tested?
Yes, test_write_rejects_field_ids_not_in_table_schema in tests/catalog/test_catalog_behaviors.py runs both cases through the four write APIs on an evolved table, checks that nothing is committed, and that appends with a renamed column's old name, reordered, promoted, missing optional and ID-less columns still work. It fails on main with DID NOT RAISE ValueError and passes with this change. test_schema_mismatch_unknown_field_ids in tests/io/test_pyarrow.py covers struct fields, list elements and map values.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes, writes now reject unknown field IDs, including dropped columns kept in Arrow data read from older Parquet files.

This pull request and its description were written by Isaac.
title: Reject columns whose field IDs are not in the table schema on write

body:
Rationale for this change
Bug: new_table_metadata reads the requested format version with properties.pop("format-version", ...) on the dict passed to create_table, so the caller's dict loses the key. For example, reusing a v1 properties dict with the SQL catalog creates the second table as v2:
properties = {"format-version": "1", "owner": "etl"}
catalog.create_table("db.events_2024", schema, properties=properties).format_version  # 1
catalog.create_table("db.events_2025", schema, properties=properties).format_version  # 2
properties  # {'owner': 'etl'}
create_table_transaction removes the key before the commit, and create_table_if_not_exists also removes it when the table exists. The pop is from #411, to keep format-version out of the persisted table properties.
Fix: pop from a copy. The Glue and DynamoDB create_table wrote the caller's dict to the Glue parameters and the DynamoDB item after this call, so they relied on the pop; they now write the new metadata's properties, as Glue's commit_table does. That also turns the values into strings there: Glue stores True as true, and DynamoDB accepts non-string values instead of failing with ParamValidationError.
Java: the BaseMetastoreCatalog table builder copies the properties into its own map, and TableMetadata.newTableMetadata reads the version with PropertyUtil.propertyAsInt and persists a new filtered map, so the caller's map is never changed.

Java's persistedProperties leaves out all reserved properties (uuid, snapshot-count, ...); new_table_metadata still only leaves out format-version.

Are these changes tested?
Yes, test_create_v1_tables_with_shared_properties in tests/catalog/test_catalog_behaviors.py, test_new_table_metadata_does_not_change_properties in tests/table/test_metadata.py and test_create_v1_table in tests/catalog/test_dynamodb.py fail on main (the dict loses format-version, or the versions are [1, 2, 2]) and pass with this change. test_create_v1_table and test_create_table_s3tables in tests/catalog/test_glue.py now check the exact Glue parameters.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes, create_table no longer changes the passed properties dict, and the Glue and DynamoDB catalogs write the property values as strings when creating a table.
