body:
Rationale for this change
Bug: _determine_partitions reads the partition source from the input by its full name in the current table schema, split on dots, while the writer follows the table's struct path with the input's own names (task_schema, from the Arrow field IDs or the name mapping). That gives two bugs:

A dot in a name on the path to a nested source fails the write. With a struct a.b and an identity partition on its child c, append raises KeyError: 'Field "a" does not exist in schema', because the split (from #2204) looks for a column a.
When the input has field IDs from before a rename, the partition values come from another column than the one the writer stores, so filtered scans miss the rows:

schema = Schema(NestedField(1, "a", StringType()), NestedField(2, "b", StringType()))
spec = PartitionSpec(PartitionField(source_id=1, field_id=1000, transform=IdentityTransform(), name="a_part"))
tbl = catalog.create_table("db.t", schema=schema, partition_spec=spec)
df = pa.Table.from_pylist([{"a": "x", "b": "y"}], schema=tbl.schema().as_arrow())  # field IDs 1 and 2
for old, new in [("a", "tmp"), ("b", "a"), ("tmp", "b")]:
    with tbl.update_schema() as update:
        update.rename_column(old, new)
tbl.append(df)
tbl.scan().to_arrow().to_pylist()  # [{'b': 'x', 'a': 'y'}]
[task.file.partition for task in tbl.scan().plan_files()]  # [Record[y]], expected [Record[x]]
tbl.scan(row_filter="b = 'x'").to_arrow().to_pylist()  # [], expected the row
Fix: find the source the same way as the writer, following its struct path in the table schema with each name taken from the input schema, and pass the names to Arrow literally. How the writer matches columns is unchanged. An input without the partition source's field ID now raises a ValueError, instead of a KeyError or a wrong partition value.
Java: SparkWriteBuilder aligns the input schema's IDs with the table, and SparkWrite reuses a PartitionKey whose StructTransform reads each row through schema.accessorForField(sourceId) of that input schema.
Not covered here: dynamic partition overwrite still has #4196 (open fix #4204), and the row filter converter (_ConvertToArrowExpression._get_field_name) also splits names, so delete rewrites and filtered scans of add_files files with dotted struct names can still raise ArrowInvalid.
Are these changes tested?
Yes, test_append_to_identity_partitioned_table_with_dotted_names, test_append_with_field_ids_after_swapping_column_names and test_partition_values_follow_writer_struct_path in tests/catalog/test_catalog_behaviors.py, and test_partition_for_nested_field_with_dotted_names in tests/io/test_pyarrow.py. On main the dotted-name tests fail with the KeyError above and the swap test with partition y instead of x; all pass with this change.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes, writes to tables partitioned on a nested field with a dot in a name on its path work, and partition values match the written data when the input has field IDs from before a rename.

This pull request and its description were written by Isaac.
title: Find partition source columns the same way as the writer

body:
Rationale for this change
Nested fields were downgraded to counts-only statistics in writer stats planning, so struct columns could not be pruned on bounds. That matters for schemas such as GeoParquet, which keep bounding boxes in struct fields.
Add write.metadata.metrics.max-inferred-column-defaults (default 100) and apply write.metadata.metrics.default to at most that many primitive fields, mirroring Java's MetricsConfig. With the limit in place, nested fields collect the same bounds as top-level fields.
Behavior details:

If write.metadata.metrics.default is set explicitly, it still applies to every column.
write.metadata.metrics.column.* overrides still apply to columns beyond the limit.
A negative limit falls back to 100.

Are these changes tested?
Yes. New tests cover the limit, overrides beyond the limit, the explicit default bypassing the limit, and the negative fallback. Existing stats tests were updated to expect nested bounds. tests/io/test_pyarrow_stats.py, tests/table, and the local write tests pass.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes. Nested columns now collect bounds by default, and tables with more than 100 primitive columns stop collecting inferred metrics beyond the first 100 unless they configure a default mode or per-column overrides.
title: Core: Control inferred column metrics and collect nested bounds

body:

body:
Part of #4078.
Rationale for this change
JSON single-value conversion had no handler for timestamp_ns and timestamptz_ns, so loading a V3 metadata file with a nanosecond initial-default raised TypeError: Cannot deserialize bytes, type timestamp_ns not supported.
Python datetime cannot hold nanoseconds, so these values are parsed as nanoseconds since epoch and formatted back as ISO-8601 with nine fractional digits. This preserves the exact value instead of truncating to microseconds.
Are these changes tested?

body:
Rationale for this change
Currently, if using an InMemoryCatalog (in-memory sqlite catalog) in a worker thread, closing or garbage collecting in the main thread raises an sqlite3.ProgrammingError. SQLAlchemy's Pool._close_connection() catches the exception, logs an ERROR traceback on sqlalchemy.pool, and leaves the underlying sqlite3.Connection open, which subsequently emits ResourceWarning: unclosed database when garbage collection occurs (Python 3.13+).
This PR sets the check_same_thread connection argument to default to False to allow the connection to be closed and garbage collection to occur.
Are these changes tested?
Yes -- see new tests:

close / garbage collection from a different thread succeeds
other operations remain single-thread only
explicit check_same_thread params are respected

Are there any user-facing changes?
No API changes.

body:
Closes #4467
Rationale for this change
_cast_if_needed relabels a UTC alias (+00:00, Etc/UTC, Z) to UTC for timestamptz
columns but not for timestamptz_ns. A table whose files come from writers that label UTC

Rationale for this change
SqlCatalog.drop_namespace only checks for tables. With namespaces a and a.b, drop_namespace("a") deletes the properties of a and returns, while a is still listed and still exists through its child. InMemoryCatalog inherits this.
Java's JdbcCatalog.dropNamespace throws NamespaceNotEmptyException when listNamespaces(namespace) is not empty. This change does the same and raises NamespaceNotEmptyError.
Are these changes tested?

Ran here: the namespace tests in tests/catalog/test_catalog_behaviors.py, tests/catalog/test_sql.py and tests/cli/test_console.py (258 passed), plus ruff, ruff-format and mypy on the changed files. The full suites are left to CI.

body:
Rationale for this change
A commit that sets main more than once adds every one of those snapshots to the snapshot log. Table.overwrite does this when it commits a delete and an append together, so time travel can resolve to the delete snapshot, which was never the committed state of the table:
table.append(pa.table({"x": [1]}))
table.overwrite(pa.table({"x": [2]}))

_, delete, _ = table.snapshots()
snapshot = table.snapshot_as_of_timestamp(delete.timestamp_ms)
table.scan(snapshot_id=snapshot.snapshot_id).to_arrow()  # no rows, expected x = 1
This happens in catalogs where PyIceberg applies the updates itself. Java's TableMetadata.Builder suppresses these entries (intermediateSnapshotIdSet and updateSnapshotLog). This change does the same: snapshots that are added and set as main, but are not current once all updates are applied, are removed from the log. They stay in snapshots.
Are these changes tested?
Yes, with a unit test on update_table_metadata and a test that overwrites a table in the memory and SQL catalogs. Both fail without the fix.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes. Table.history() and inspect.history() have one entry for a commit that replaces its own snapshots, and snapshot_as_of_timestamp no longer returns the replaced ones. Tables that already have such entries in their log are not rewritten.
title: Leave intermediate snapshots out of the snapshot log

Closes #1169
Rationale for this change
PyArrow pa.time64("ns") was unsupported on write and raised Unsupported type: time64[ns], even though Iceberg's time type is microsecond precision by spec. Users had to manually downcast a time64[ns] column before writing, while the analogous timestamp[ns] case has been handled by an opt-in downcast since #848.
This change mirrors that existing ns -> us timestamp behavior for time, gated on the same downcast-ns-timestamp-to-us-on-write configuration property:

pyiceberg/io/pyarrow.py, _ConvertToIceberg.primitive: a time64[ns] PyArrow type now maps to Iceberg TimeType() (with a warning) when downcast-ns-timestamp-to-us-on-write is set, and otherwise raises a TypeError pointing the user at that property. time64[us] keeps working unchanged.
pyiceberg/io/pyarrow.py, ArrowProjectionVisitor._cast_if_needed: a new TimeType branch casts a time64[ns] array to time64[us] (safe=False) on write when the flag is set, so the data, not just the schema mapping, is actually downcast.
Tests: updated test_pyarrow_time64_ns_to_iceberg and added test_pyarrow_time64_ns_to_iceberg_downcast, test__to_requested_schema_time_ns_downcast, and test__to_requested_schema_time_ns_without_downcast_raises_exception.

Are these changes tested?
Yes — pytest tests/io/test_pyarrow_visitor.py tests/io/test_pyarrow.py passes (296 passed, 3 skipped), including the 3 new tests and the updated one. ruff check and ruff format --check pass on all changed files.

body:
Rationale for this change
null_value_counts is optional in a data file. When a file has none, Java's StrictMetricsEvaluator treats every column as possibly containing nulls:
private boolean canContainNulls(Integer id) {
  return nullCounts == null || (nullCounts.containsKey(id) && nullCounts.get(id) > 0);
}
_StrictMetricsEvaluationVisitor._can_contain_nulls read the missing map as empty, so it treated every column as having no nulls. For an optional column x with bounds 1 to 5 and no null counts, x < 10, x <= 5, x > 0 and x >= 1 returned ROWS_MUST_MATCH, although rows where x is null do not match.
_DeleteFiles drops a data file when the strict evaluator returns ROWS_MUST_MATCH, so for such a file delete("x < 10") also removed the rows where x is null.
Now the visitor treats every column as possibly containing nulls when the file has no null value counts, as Java does. A file whose map exists but has no entry for a column is unchanged, which also matches Java.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_strict_missing_null_counts in tests/expressions/test_evaluator.py checks the four predicates on the same file with null counts {1: 0} (must match) and without null counts (might not match). It fails without the change. The rest of tests/expressions passes, apart from two test_parser.py cases and the Cython-decoder warning tests that fail the same way on main in my environment. ruff and ruff format are clean on the changed files, and mypy reports nothing new.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Deletes no longer drop a whole data file without null value counts when the predicate cannot match its null rows. Such a file is now read and rewritten, so only the matching rows are removed.
title: Treat missing null value counts as unknown in the strict metrics evaluator

body:
Rationale for this change
Requesting dictionary encoding on a streaming scan dropped the Iceberg field ID for that column. Saving the result to Parquet preserved the values but lost the column's identity. The same export without dictionary encoding kept the ID.
The reader now takes the dictionary type from the first batch and retains the field from the projected schema. The encoding fix in #3595 still applies.
Are these changes tested?
End-to-end testing
With the PyArrow and SQLite extras installed, run the reproducer from the checkout:
PYTHONPATH=. python -B repro.py

Before, the dictionary-enabled column could not be converted back to an Iceberg field. Output and final exception:
dictionary=False, field ID=b'2'
round-trip field ID=2, rows=2
dictionary=True, field ID=None
ValueError: Parquet file does not have field-ids and the Iceberg table does not have 'schema.name-mapping.default' defined

After:
dictionary=False, field ID=b'2'
round-trip field ID=2, rows=2
dictionary=True, field ID=b'2'
round-trip field ID=2, rows=2

Reproducer source: repro.py
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.parquet as pq
from pyiceberg.catalog.sql import SqlCatalog
from pyiceberg.io.pyarrow import PYARROW_PARQUET_FIELD_ID_KEY, pyarrow_to_schema
from pyiceberg.schema import Schema
from pyiceberg.types import IntegerType, NestedField, StringType

with TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    directory = Path(tmp)
    catalog = SqlCatalog("demo", uri="sqlite://", warehouse=directory.as_uri())
    catalog.create_namespace("demo")
    table = catalog.create_table(
        identifier="demo.samples",
        schema=Schema(NestedField(1, "id", IntegerType()), NestedField(2, "kind", StringType())),
    )
    table.append(pa.table({"id": pa.array([1, 2], type=pa.int32()), "kind": ["a", "b"]}))
    for columns in [(), ("kind",)]:
        rows = table.scan().to_arrow_batch_reader(dictionary_columns=columns).read_all()
        field = rows.schema.field("kind")
        print(f"dictionary={pa.types.is_dictionary(field.type)}, field ID={(field.metadata or {}).get(PYARROW_PARQUET_FIELD_ID_KEY)}")
        path = directory / "scan.parquet"
        pq.write_table(table=rows, where=path)
        converted = pyarrow_to_schema(pq.read_schema(path))
        print(f"round-trip field ID={converted.find_field('kind').field_id}, rows={rows.num_rows}")

Are there any user-facing changes?
Parquet exports from dictionary-enabled batch scans keep the same field IDs as plain scans.
AI disclosure: GitHub Copilot CLI drafted the fix and regression assertion.
title: PyArrow: Preserve field IDs on dictionary batch reads

body:
Rationale for this change
Bug: removing a partition field and adding it back with the same source, transform and name in one update should leave the spec unchanged. PyIceberg adds a new field instead:
# format-version 1, partition by identity(region) (field id 1000)
tbl.update_spec().remove_field("region").add_identity("region").commit()
# spec: [1000 "region_1000" void, 1001 "region" identity], default spec id 1
# expected: [1000 "region" identity], default spec id 0
On format-version 2, when the field is not the last one, the re-added field moves to the end and a new spec is written.
Fix: add_field keeps the removed field, with its id and position, when it is added back with the same name, source and transform. This matches Java's rewriteDeleteAndAddField. A time transform restored after another time transform was added in the same update is accepted too, as in Java; main raises Cannot add time partition field.
Java callers: Spark's REPLACE PARTITION FIELD converts SQL transforms to Iceberg terms and removes/adds in one update; Flink's TableUpdater does this for PartitionSpecEvolution's diff of the current and requested specs. This PR covers Python's update_spec().
Re-adds under another name and unnamed re-adds after a new field takes the removed name retain main's behaviour. Java restores and renames the removed field in these cases; that remains a follow-up.
Builds on #4110 (partition field ID reuse on v3 tables) and #4307 (a new field can take a removed field's name).
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_update_spec_remove_and_add_same_field_in_one_update (v1 and v2, first and last field), test_update_spec_remove_field_added_back_in_same_update (removing the field again) and test_update_spec_restore_time_transform_after_added_time_transform (both add orders, v1 and v2) fail on main and pass with this change. test_update_spec_add_field_with_new_name_after_remove (a re-add under another name, and a swap of two removed names) and test_update_spec_add_field_conflicts_with_added_field (a name or a transform already added in the update) pass on main and with this change, so they pin main's behaviour. test_update_spec_remove_and_add_renamed_field_in_one_update (a field renamed in an earlier update, restored under its new name, then a later add of that name) fails on main and passes with this change. test_update_spec_remove_and_add_same_field_reuses_id gains a v1 case, which fails on main.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes. Removing and re-adding the same source, transform and name in one update preserves the spec (no void field on v1, no new spec id). Restoring a removed time transform after another time transform was added in the same update now works (Java accepts; main raises). Re-adds under a different name are unchanged from main. An unnamed re-add keeps the current partition name, as Java does. Main generated a default name on v1 or could reuse a historical name on v2/v3. A later add can no longer take the restored name.
This pull request and its description were written by Isaac.
title: Undelete a partition field re-added in the same update

body:
Rationale for this change
Bug: a snapshot can have no summary, and then it has no operation. The summary is optional in v1, and a v1 table upgraded to v2 keeps such snapshots. Table.inspect.snapshots() then shows the text "None" as the operation:
# tbl is a format v1 table whose snapshot has no summary
tbl.inspect.snapshots().column("operation").to_pylist()
# ['None'], expected [None]
snapshots() sets operation = None in this case, then stores str(operation) in the nullable column.
Fix: store operation as is, so a missing summary gives a null cell. summary is already null.
Java: Spark's .snapshots scan uses SnapshotsTable, which returns the operation parsed by SnapshotParser unchanged, including null (TestSnapshotJson checks the null). This PR fixes the equivalent PyIceberg inspection output.
Still different from Java, not changed here: "summary": {} reads as operation overwrite (with a warning, as in Summary), while Java reads it as no summary.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_inspect_snapshots_operation_is_null_without_summary in tests/table/test_inspect.py builds a v1 table, removes the summary from its snapshot in the metadata file, and checks that operation is null. It fails on main with ['None'] where [None] is expected, and passes with this change. The v2 control still reports append.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes, operation is null instead of the string None for snapshots without a summary. Please add the changelog label.
This pull request and its description were written by Isaac.
title: Return null operation for snapshots without a summary
